title: When Your Best Engineer Is Hard to Work With
summary: Fast, skilled and hard to work with. What research says about the cost of one harmful teammate, why teams keep paying it, and how to set boundaries with room to repair.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
It's 4 p.m. and production has been broken since lunch. Customers are waiting and the incident channel is scrolling fast. Then one engineer spots the missing condition, pushes a fix straight to main, and the dashboard turns green. The channel fills with thank-yous.

Over the next hour, different messages show up in DMs. The fix skipped review. Two people felt talked over on the call. A junior engineer had pointed at the same clue an hour earlier, got told "that's not it," and says next time they'll keep it to themselves.

That's the pattern people mean by "toxic rockstar" or "brilliant jerk." I don't love either label, because it turns a person into a verdict and makes a management problem sound like a personality test. The pattern is real, though: lots of visible output, plus damage that's harder to see. Trust thins, feedback arrives later, the less assertive people pull back, and every important decision costs a little more.

Why teams keep making the deal

The confusing part is that the work is often genuinely strong. This person debugs fast, knows the codebase cold, rescues releases and holds context other people still need. So the team hesitates. Pushing back on someone who ships feels wasteful. Upsetting the one person who knows where the fragile parts are feels risky. Nobody says it out loud, but the team accepts a deal: high output in exchange for rough behavior.

Managers are usually part of that deal, even when they dislike the behavior. We celebrate the person who saved the release louder than the people whose work meant the next release didn't need saving. We praise speed without asking who cleaned up after it. We count "ownership" toward promotion without checking whether it turned into a private kingdom. The values page says collaboration. The promo packet follows the metrics.

What one person can cost

The deal is more expensive than it looks, and there's research on why.

Will Felps, an organizational behavior researcher, ran an experiment where groups of four students spent about 45 minutes on a management decision task, with $100 per person for the best team. One "member" was an actor named Nick, playing a jerk, a slacker or a depressive pessimist. As This American Life reported it, across dozens of trials, groups where Nick played the bad apple performed 30% to 40% worse than groups without one, even when the others were talented. What surprised Felps more was how people treated each other: they argued, communicated less and stopped sharing relevant information.

A much larger dataset points the same way. Michael Housman and Dylan Minor studied more than 50,000 frontline service workers across 11 firms, and they defined "toxic" narrowly: fired for an egregious policy violation such as harassment, fraud or workplace violence (Toxic Workers, Harvard Business School working paper, 2015). Those workers were actually faster than their peers, which is exactly why they're tempting to keep. But the turnover they triggered among coworkers alone cost about $12,489 per toxic worker, while a top 1% performer saved about $5,303. Their conclusion: avoiding a toxic worker, or bringing one up to average, pays off by more than two to one compared with hiring a superstar.

Neither study looked at software teams, and an engineer who talks over people in design review is a long way from fraud. The mechanism will still look familiar from your own repo: everyone else absorbs the cost, and it shows up as missing information.

Engineering teams run on early signals: a half-formed worry in planning, a junior's awkward question, a reviewer saying the abstraction isn't clear yet, an on-call engineer admitting they're not sure. When a high-status person keeps punishing those signals, the team loses data along with goodwill. The next bug shows up later, and fewer people are willing to name it early.

Name the behavior, skip the label

"They're toxic" is a conclusion, and nobody can act on a conclusion. Start with what you saw and what it did:

  • "In yesterday's design review you interrupted Linh three times before she finished explaining the proposal. She didn't speak again for the rest of the meeting."
  • "In the last two incidents you merged to main without a second reviewer. Both fixes worked, and both times the on-call engineer couldn't tell what had changed."
  • "In planning you called Minh's concern obvious. He hasn't raised one in that meeting since."

Being specific helps both sides. The person getting the feedback has something real to look at instead of a label to argue with, and the team can't hide a vague grudge behind a big word. If you want a structure for the conversation itself, this script for hard feedback walks through one.

Room to repair, same rules

Two things get mixed up here. A repair path says: we believe this can change, and here's what better looks like. Permission says: you're valuable, so the rules bend for you. A healthy team offers the first, with direct feedback, coaching and real time to improve. It never offers the second.

The boundaries that don't move:

  • No put-downs in public, whether in meetings, threads or review comments.
  • No skipping review unless the team has declared an emergency, and emergency changes get reviewed afterward.
  • No private ownership of shared systems. Context gets written down and shared.
  • No payback when someone disagrees.

Netflix's culture page puts it bluntly: "No matter how brilliant someone may be, there's no place in our Dream Team for people who don't treat their colleagues with decency and respect" (Netflix Culture). You don't need the rest of Netflix's playbook to borrow that sentence.

Put the boundary in the workflow

A boundary that lives only in a 1:1 fades fast. Put it where the work happens. If review is required, turn on branch protection so skipping it takes a visible override. If incident reviews are blameless, the facilitator stops blame in the room as it happens. Google's SRE book says a blameless postmortem looks for contributing causes "without indicting any individual or team," because where finger-pointing wins, "people will not bring issues to light for fear of punishment" (Postmortem Culture). That rule protects the fast fixer, and it also means they don't get to blame anyone else. If one person holds all the context on a critical system, schedule pairing, docs and an on-call rotation until the system stops depending on one person's memory.

Culture changes when the default path changes. There's more on that in the post on blameless culture.

Look after the people around it

Leaders sometimes spend all their energy on the difficult high performer and forget the people who've been absorbing the cost. Those teammates need visible proof that speaking up wasn't a career mistake: their work recognized in public, their concerns followed up, their boundaries respected. Otherwise they learn the unofficial rule, that the real standard is whatever the most valuable person can get away with.

Felps' experiment had one hopeful exception. A single group did well despite Nick. One member kept asking questions, pulled every teammate into the discussion and defused conflict as soon as it started. (He turned out to be a diplomat's son.) You don't need diplomatic training to do those three things in your next meeting.

If nothing changes

None of this means casting the high performer as a villain. Many people picked up rough habits in places that rewarded rescues, speed, certainty and being irreplaceable. Some are honestly surprised when they hear the impact laid out. Some repair well once the feedback is specific and the boundaries hold. Some don't.

You can't predict how someone will turn out, and you don't have to. What you can do is make the current impact visible, agree on what better looks like and by when, write it down, and decide how much the team can reasonably absorb while the repair is attempted. If the date comes and nothing has moved, remember the Housman and Minor numbers: a fast but harmful teammate is rarely the bargain they look like.

Try this week

  • Write down one specific behavior, and its impact, that you've been filing under "that's just how they are."
  • Check whether your main branch really requires review, and who can bypass it.
  • Thank, in public, one person who raised a concern that turned out to matter.
  • In your next tense meeting, ask the person who hasn't spoken yet what they think.

faqs.q: What is a "brilliant jerk" or "toxic rockstar" on an engineering team?
faqs.a: Someone whose individual output is high but whose behavior damages the people around them: talking over others, skipping review, dismissing concerns or hoarding context. The output is easy to see. The cost shows up later as thinner trust, slower feedback and teammates who stop raising issues.

faqs.q: Does one difficult teammate really hurt team performance?
faqs.a: In Will Felps' experiment, described on This American Life, groups with an actor playing a jerk, slacker or pessimist performed 30% to 40% worse, and members shared less information. Housman and Minor's study of over 50,000 service workers found that avoiding a toxic worker paid off more than twice as much as hiring a top 1% performer. Neither study looked at software teams specifically.

faqs.q: How do I give feedback to a high performer whose behavior is a problem?
faqs.a: Skip labels like "toxic" and describe what happened and what it caused: "You interrupted Linh three times in the design review, and she didn't speak again." Make clear what better looks like, offer coaching and time, and keep the same rules that apply to everyone else.

faqs.q: What boundaries should apply to everyone, including top performers?
faqs.a: No public put-downs, no skipping review outside a declared emergency, no private ownership of shared systems, and no retaliation when someone disagrees. Put them into the workflow too: branch protection, blameless incident reviews and shared on-call.

faqs.q: What if the behavior doesn't change?
faqs.a: Agree on specific changes and a date, write them down, and protect the teammates who have been absorbing the cost in the meantime. If nothing has moved by the date, act on it. In Housman and Minor's data, keeping a toxic worker cost the firm more than their extra speed was worth.
